prompt.brief: Design an incident-management platform that detects and correlates signals into actionable incidents, maps blast radius, recommends evidence-backed remediation, coordinates responders, and learns from outcomes.
successSignals: Define signal identity, incident lifecycle, service ownership/topology, severity, evidence, responders, runbooks, confidence, and audit history.
Correlate alerts without hiding raw evidence, identify affected services, route escalation, and distinguish suggestions from approved actions.
Separate detection/routing from enrichment, collaboration, remediation execution, postmortems, and learning; make all transitions idempotent.
Explain noisy/missing signals, false grouping, privacy, access, replay, observability, and manual fallback.

functional: Ingest signals, open/update incidents, correlate evidence, calculate severity/blast radius, notify responders, and track acknowledgments/resolution.
Recommend runbooks and owners, coordinate tasks, record approved actions, generate timelines/postmortems, and learn from operator feedback.
Support incident merge/split, suppression windows, audit/export, deletion policies, replay, and recovery after notification or enrichment failure.
nonFunctional: Open high-confidence incidents within two minutes while preserving raw signals and clearly labeling uncertain recommendations.
Handle 1M alerts per hour across 50k services without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Incident-management platform commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Incident-management platform writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Incident-management platform version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Incident-management platform by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Incident-management platform work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Incident-management platform projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Incident-management platform projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Incident-management platform records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Incident-management platform latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
